decision: lab-agent is delivered by the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor@v1); it keeps only its declaration, build scripts, PKGBUILD, public key and install test.
why: Its delivery workflows were a near copy of snapall's; copies drift and fixes do not travel.
rejected: Keeping its own copy of the delivery machinery.

decision: lab-agent records each wait itself - start, end, what is waited on, the project - and requires both on a waiting submit; a gatherer brings the waits into each project's data.
why: Capture must be unavoidable and cost nothing: the place every wait happens is lab-agent's own wait.
rejected: Logging waits by hand (it would be skipped); estimating them afterwards.

decision: oco-agent is built inside lab-agent's repository (oco-agent/), tested by its CI and kept out of its releases, until it takes over and the repository takes its name.
why: Its design, research and backlog already live here; lab-agent must keep serving while it is proven; tad's Rust version grew the same way.
rejected: A new repository now (the reasoning and the code would live apart, and the history would split).

decision: Each driver - a person or a machine - has a lease of its own, kept alive by its beats: a job starts only while the driver who asked for it is still there. Beats are what is known now, not a history: one fact per driver, a newer beat replacing an older and never the reverse; they are kept apart from the journal, behind their own port, with their own check in the measure.
why: oco-agent coordinates work for any driver; one driver going silent must not stop another's work, and must stop its own. Beats arrive often and only the latest matters, so they are state, where the journal is history.
rejected: One lease for 'the' driver (the first design: a silent AI would have stopped the author's work too); beats as journal entries (hundreds of lines a day that say nothing after the next one).

decision: The redesigned lab-agent is oco-agent: born beside lab-agent, which serves until the switch - as tad's Rust version grew beside the Python one - then lab-agent retires.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: it is tied to ocoeco by design. 'agent' is the established word for this role; 'oco-' names its family and its dependency on ocoeco.
rejected: runner (GitHub's word - true, but it says nothing of the voice, the journal or the leases); keeping lab-agent (it names a place, not what it belongs to); renaming in place (the old one must keep serving until the new one is proven).

decision: lab-agent's core speaks its own language and depends on nothing outside itself (a crate with no input or output); every technology - git and GitHub, ntfy, systemd - is an adapter behind a port the core defines, and its words appear nowhere above it; areas are named for what lab-agent is for; the playbook's guards check it on every change; in-memory adapters run the chaos tests. The journal is declared tad tables queried with SQL, and where they live is itself an adapter; finished work becomes glimpses. The journal's SQL is tad's, and tad's SQL is DuckDB's (tad-engine 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb), as tad's original research decided.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: follow the ideal-project guidelines; the implementation must not rely on GitHub - it is today's adapter, and switching it (to Redis, say) must be a clean replacement; git as a heap of files is a one-off mess when tad is a database and ocoeco makes every action intelligible.
rejected: A core that calls GitHub and git directly (the prototype's way, and the root of the incident's reach); folders named ports and adapters (the playbook: names say what the program is for); the journal as files in a repository with no declaration.

decision: oco-agent is trusted with nothing until it has watched lab-agent: a shadow run reads lab-agent's newest log every ten minutes through oco-agent's rules, keeps its own journal, and alerts urgently when lab-agent starts work oco-agent would have refused. It decides; it never acts.
why: Rules proven on tests and on one night's log should also hold on the days that follow, before they run anything; and lab-agent is still the one running jobs, so a replay there must be noticed at once.
rejected: Switching to oco-agent at once (proven only on the past); a daily report (a replay storm ran 102 jobs in twenty minutes on 2026-11-11).

decision: lab-agent is redesigned around a journal per job, run-once by construction, the driver's lease with park-on-silence, each job's heartbeat, flows of idempotent steps that resume, a working tree per job and side-by-side by resource, crash-only recovery, a watcher outside the machine, secrets kept out of URLs, and its data flowing through ocoeco - in five stages, each proven by chaos tests before the next (DESIGN.md). Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-ports-names-and-tables: ports and adapters with the playbook's names and guards, and the journal as tad tables queried with SQL.
why: The 2026-11-11 incident traced to a foundation laid as a one-off prototype; the author asked for the best the world has learned, with the full picture in mind.
rejected: Patching the replay and carrying on (the other paths stay open); adopting a durable-execution engine such as Temporal or Restate (a server to run and secure on one machine with no inbound port - lab-agent takes their proven ideas into a small core instead, with git as the record it already has).
